scenarios.name: No one is answerable for fraud risk
scenarios.how: Gaps persist because nobody owns fraud risk or has the authority to act.
scenarios.why: Without a named, accountable person, other controls decay unnoticed.

scenarios.name: Fraud by owners or senior people goes unchallenged
scenarios.how: An owner or executive overrides controls, or an allegation against them reaches only the people implicated.
scenarios.why: Management override is the route that ordinary controls do not stop.

scenarios.name: The oversight body never sees fraud risk
scenarios.how: Those with final oversight receive no reporting, so losses and weaknesses are not challenged.
scenarios.why: Oversight cannot act on fraud risk it never hears about.

scenarios.name: Group oversight leaves no one accountable locally
scenarios.how: Each side assumes the other is managing fraud risk in the subsidiary.
scenarios.why: Local accountability stops group oversight from becoming nobody's job.

scenarios.name: The response to a discovered fraud is improvised
scenarios.how: Evidence is lost, the wrong people are told and recovery is delayed in the first days.
scenarios.why: The first days of a case decide what can be proved and recovered.

scenarios.name: The PRECCA section 34 reporting duty is missed
scenarios.how: A manager in a position of authority fails to report a corruption, fraud, theft, extortion or forgery matter of R100 000 or more.
scenarios.why: Failing to report is an offence in its own right.

scenarios.name: Suspicious transactions are not reported to the FIC
scenarios.how: A business does not report a suspicious or unusual transaction under section 29 of FICA, or an accountable institution fails its wider duties.
scenarios.why: Section 29 applies to every business; accountable institutions carry further duties.

scenarios.name: A public body has no fraud prevention plan
scenarios.how: Internal audit and management effort is not directed at fraud risk.
scenarios.why: A regulatory expectation for PFMA institutions, and part of municipal risk management.

scenarios.name: Not ready for the coming cybercrime reporting duty
scenarios.how: A financial institution or communications provider cannot report within 72 hours once section 54 is in operation.

scenarios.name: Automated decisions are manipulated without a human check
scenarios.how: AI tools that approve, pay or onboard are fed false inputs and act at scale.
scenarios.why: Manipulated automation fails at scale before anyone notices.

scenarios.name: Bribery liability without procedures to prevent it
scenarios.how: A person acting for the organisation pays a bribe and the organisation has no procedures to show.

scenarios.name: Approval limits and exceptions are not controlled
scenarios.how: Payments, contracts or bank changes are approved by people without authority, or exceptions are self-approved.

scenarios.name: Lessons are not learned after a fraud
scenarios.how: The same weakness allows the next fraud.

scenarios.name: Insurance does not pay when a fraud is claimed
scenarios.how: Cover is missing, excludes impersonation fraud, or a condition is breached.

scenarios.name: Unapproved AI tools leak confidential information
scenarios.how: Staff paste financial, customer or employee data into tools not approved for it.

scenarios.name: Fraud risks are never identified
scenarios.how: Management does not know how fraud could happen in its own processes.
scenarios.why: Whether risks are understood decides whether controls are aimed at the right schemes.

scenarios.name: AI-enabled schemes are not considered
scenarios.how: Deepfake instructions, synthetic identities and generated documents are missing from management's view of fraud risk.
scenarios.why: These schemes defeat controls that rely on recognising a person or a document.

scenarios.name: Recognised risks are not tied to controls
scenarios.how: The organisation cannot show which control would stop or detect each scheme it knows about.
scenarios.why: Risks that are not linked to controls cannot be shown to be managed.

scenarios.name: Key controls are assumed to work but never tested
scenarios.how: A control exists on paper but has stopped operating.

scenarios.name: Risks above tolerance are left without action
scenarios.how: Assessment results do not change controls, audit work or training.

scenarios.name: The assessment goes stale as the business changes
scenarios.how: New products, structures and threats are not assessed.

scenarios.name: Bribes are paid or accepted, directly or through others
scenarios.how: Staff or intermediaries offer or accept gratification to win or retain business.
scenarios.why: PRECCA criminalises bribery in both sectors, including bribes paid through others.

scenarios.name: Undeclared conflicts steer decisions
scenarios.how: A person with an undisclosed interest approves a supplier, customer or payment.
scenarios.why: Undeclared interests sit behind most procurement and approval fraud.

scenarios.name: Bids are rigged with competitors
scenarios.how: Prices or who will bid are agreed with competitors on public-sector work.
scenarios.why: Collusive tendering is prohibited under the Competition Act and taints the contract.

scenarios.name: Public servants do business with the state
scenarios.how: Employees hold undeclared interests in suppliers to the state.
scenarios.why: Public servants may not conduct business with the state.

scenarios.name: Extortion at projects and sites turns into bribery
scenarios.how: Payments demanded at sites are made informally and unrecorded.
scenarios.why: Unmanaged payments under pressure can become bribery.

scenarios.name: Foreign agents pay bribes
scenarios.how: Distributors or agents abroad pay officials on the organisation's behalf.
scenarios.why: Foreign agents are the most common route for cross-border bribery.

scenarios.name: Gifts and hospitality buy influence
scenarios.how: Hospitality from parties awaiting a decision goes unrecorded.

scenarios.name: Records are falsified to meet targets or win work
scenarios.how: Staff fabricate records believing it benefits the organisation.

scenarios.name: Leaders are exempt from the rules
scenarios.how: Senior people are held to different standards, which signals that rules are optional.

scenarios.name: Staff do not know or understand what is expected
scenarios.how: Expectations are not communicated in a way people understand, and nobody checks.

scenarios.name: Donations or sponsorships channel bribes
scenarios.how: A payment to a cause linked to a decision-maker buys influence.

scenarios.name: Dealings with officials go unrecorded
scenarios.how: Contact about tenders, licences or inspections happens one-on-one and off the record.

scenarios.name: Incentives push people to cut corners
scenarios.how: Targets and bonuses reward misreporting.

scenarios.name: A fictitious supplier is created and paid
scenarios.how: An insider or outsider adds a supplier that does not exist and invoices it.
scenarios.why: Fictitious suppliers enter through onboarding that can be skipped.

scenarios.name: Supplier payments are diverted through changed bank details
scenarios.how: A fraudster, often impersonating the supplier by email, voice or video, has the bank account changed.
scenarios.why: Changed supplier bank details are the most common route for payment fraud, and cloned voices now defeat call-backs that rely on recognition.

scenarios.name: A supplier is set up with an account it does not own
scenarios.how: Payments go to an employee's or fraudster's account from the first invoice.
scenarios.why: Confirming account ownership at onboarding stops both fictitious and impersonated suppliers being paid into accounts they do not own; added after the review's isolated-weakness probe.

scenarios.name: One person can order and approve payment
scenarios.how: A buyer invents or inflates a purchase and approves its payment.
scenarios.why: One person who can both order and approve payment can pay a supplier they invented.

scenarios.name: Invoices are paid for goods or services not received or not agreed
scenarios.how: Overbilling, fictitious deliveries or inflated rates are paid.
scenarios.why: Invoices paid without checking approval and receipt are how overbilling and fictitious deliveries get paid.

scenarios.name: An outsourced provider misuses its access
scenarios.how: A provider that handles money, customers or data has wider access than the service needs.
scenarios.why: Provider access wider than the service needs is how outsourced processes are abused; now applies wherever processes are outsourced, not only where nothing is bought.

scenarios.name: Supplier payments are released without two approvals
scenarios.how: One person releases a payment run.

scenarios.name: A tender is manipulated or purchases are split
scenarios.how: Specifications, evaluation or thresholds are bent towards a chosen supplier.

scenarios.name: Buyers take kickbacks
scenarios.how: A long-standing buyer-supplier relationship hides favours.

scenarios.name: Purchase cards or petty cash are misused
scenarios.how: Personal purchases or split transactions go unreviewed.

scenarios.name: Intermediaries pay bribes or inflate fees
scenarios.how: Agents act improperly or bill for work not done.

scenarios.name: Procurement anomalies are never noticed
scenarios.how: Patterns such as splitting or duplicates go unseen.

scenarios.name: Variations inflate the agreed value
scenarios.how: Extra scope or rates are approved after the work is done.

scenarios.name: Salaries are redirected through a fake bank change
scenarios.how: A request that appears to come from an employee changes where their salary is paid.
scenarios.why: Salary redirection through fake bank change requests is common and fast.

scenarios.name: Ghost employees are paid
scenarios.how: Fictitious or departed people stay on the payroll.
scenarios.why: A payroll that nobody independent reviews before payment is where ghost employees hide.

scenarios.name: Leavers stay on the payroll
scenarios.how: A leaver keeps being paid, often to an account someone else controls.
scenarios.why: Leavers who stay on the payroll are the commonest ghost employees.

scenarios.name: A false identity enters at hiring
scenarios.how: Someone is employed under a stolen or invented identity or false qualifications.
scenarios.why: False identities enter at hiring and are hard to remove afterwards.

scenarios.name: A stand-in or deepfake candidate is appointed
scenarios.how: A remote hire is not the person who was interviewed or who does the work.
scenarios.why: Deepfake and stand-in candidates are now a recorded way into organisations.

scenarios.name: Individuals are paid without a payroll to unverified accounts
scenarios.how: Contractors or casual helpers are paid into accounts nobody confirmed.
scenarios.why: Paying individuals to bank details that have not been confirmed invites diversion.

scenarios.name: The payroll payment file is altered after approval
scenarios.how: Account numbers or amounts change between approval and the bank.

scenarios.name: Cash wages are stolen or paid to ghosts
scenarios.how: Cash pay-outs are not witnessed or reconciled.

scenarios.name: Hours and overtime are inflated
scenarios.how: Unworked hours or overtime are approved and paid.

scenarios.name: Expenses and advances are abused
scenarios.how: False or inflated claims are paid.

scenarios.name: Labour brokers invoice for workers who were not there
scenarios.how: Broker or casual worker numbers are inflated.

scenarios.name: An insider in a high-risk role works unchecked
scenarios.how: Someone who never hands over work conceals an ongoing fraud.

scenarios.name: An outsourced payroll provider acts on unverified instructions
scenarios.how: The provider accepts changes from anyone who appears to be the client.

scenarios.name: An unauthorised payment leaves the bank
scenarios.how: One person can release money, on the platform or through a branch instruction.
scenarios.why: Two-person release enforced where money leaves is the last barrier before a payment goes.

scenarios.name: A new beneficiary is paid on a fake instruction
scenarios.how: An invoice or request from an impersonator is paid to a new account.
scenarios.why: New beneficiaries are where impersonation and invoice fraud are paid out.

scenarios.name: An impersonated executive bypasses the checks
scenarios.how: An urgent, confidential request in an executive's name skips the call-back.
scenarios.why: Deepfake executive instructions succeed where seniority overrides the normal checks.

scenarios.name: A payment is hidden in the reconciliation
scenarios.how: The person who pays also reconciles, so a diverted payment is never questioned.
scenarios.why: A reconciliation prepared by the person who pays can hide the payment.

scenarios.name: Small or outsourced finance has no independent eye
scenarios.how: A bookkeeper or provider controls the money and the records.
scenarios.why: An owner's review of the statements is the main independent check in a small or outsourced set-up.

scenarios.name: Donor or grant funds are diverted or claimed twice
scenarios.how: Restricted funds are spent on other purposes or claimed from more than one funder.
scenarios.why: Funds not tracked separately can be diverted or claimed twice; now applies to any organisation with restricted funds, not only by legal form.

scenarios.name: A payment file is altered before it reaches the bank
scenarios.how: Account numbers change between approval and the bank.

scenarios.name: Bank mandates or accounts are changed without approval
scenarios.how: Signatories, users or accounts are added outside senior approval.

scenarios.name: A fraudulent payment is not recalled in time
scenarios.how: Hours are lost finding whom to call at the bank.

scenarios.name: Financial results are manipulated
scenarios.how: Results are misstated to meet bonuses, covenants or funding conditions.

scenarios.name: Journals or write-offs conceal fraud
scenarios.how: Manual entries move or remove amounts without independent approval.

scenarios.name: The SARS profile is hijacked or refunds diverted
scenarios.how: A refund is redirected after the eFiling profile or banking details are changed.

scenarios.name: Treasury deals or transfers are misused
scenarios.how: Investments or own-account transfers move money outside normal approval.

scenarios.name: Automated finance outputs are relied on unchecked
scenarios.how: A tool's reconciliation or payment proposal is released without review.

scenarios.name: Refunds are stolen
scenarios.how: One person raises and approves refunds or credit notes to themselves or accomplices.
scenarios.why: Refunds processed and approved by one person are a classic way to steal.

scenarios.name: Customer details are changed to divert money or goods
scenarios.how: Refund accounts, delivery addresses or contact numbers are changed without the customer.
scenarios.why: Changed customer details are how refunds and goods are redirected.

scenarios.name: Credit is obtained with fabricated documents
scenarios.how: Fake payslips and bank statements, now easy to generate, secure credit that is never repaid.
scenarios.why: Application fraud with fabricated documents drives credit losses.

scenarios.name: Remote onboarding is passed with a deepfake or synthetic identity
scenarios.how: Accounts are opened or payouts received by people who are not who they claim.
scenarios.why: Remote account opening without checks designed to resist deepfakes is open to synthetic identities.

scenarios.name: Claims are fabricated or inflated
scenarios.how: False warranty, guarantee or insurance claims are paid.
scenarios.why: Claims fraud is the main fraud risk for organisations that pay claims.

scenarios.name: Income is skimmed where there are no sales
scenarios.how: Rent, fees or other income is collected and recorded by the same person.
scenarios.why: Income that is collected and recorded by the same person can be skimmed.

scenarios.name: Public fees are skimmed at collection
scenarios.how: Fees, fines or levies are collected in a system the collector can alter.
scenarios.why: Fees collected in a system the collector can alter are easily skimmed.

scenarios.name: Customer due diligence fails
scenarios.how: An accountable institution onboards customers without the required due diligence.
scenarios.why: Customer due diligence is a legal duty for accountable institutions.

scenarios.name: Sales are not billed or receipts are diverted
scenarios.how: Goods or services are provided without an invoice, or payments are taken off the books.

scenarios.name: Customers pay fraudsters impersonating the organisation
scenarios.how: Customers receive fake banking details and pay the wrong account.

scenarios.name: Prices are overridden or side deals made
scenarios.how: Discounts or terms favour a customer in return for a kickback.

scenarios.name: Agents report fictitious sales
scenarios.how: Commission is paid on customers who do not exist or soon cancel.

scenarios.name: Vouchers and loyalty points are abused
scenarios.how: Staff issue or redeem value to themselves or associates.

scenarios.name: Customers are wrongly blocked on a fraud flag
scenarios.how: An automated flag is treated as proof and a customer is penalised without review.

scenarios.name: Cash takings are stolen
scenarios.how: Takings are under-recorded or removed before banking.
scenarios.why: Daily reconciliation of takings is the main control over cash theft.

scenarios.name: Stock is stolen and hidden in the counts
scenarios.how: The people who hold stock also count it.
scenarios.why: Counts done by the people who hold the stock can hide its theft.

scenarios.name: Portable and fixed assets go missing
scenarios.how: Laptops, tools or equipment disappear without being noticed.

scenarios.name: Data leaves on disposed or reissued devices
scenarios.how: Devices are sold, reissued or returned without being wiped.

scenarios.name: Assets or scrap are sold off cheaply or without payment
scenarios.how: Disposals favour insiders or goods leave before payment.

scenarios.name: Goods are released to an impostor
scenarios.how: A changed delivery or collection instruction sends goods to a fraudster.

scenarios.name: Fuel and fleet are misused
scenarios.how: Fuel cards or vehicles are used privately or fraudulently.

scenarios.name: Goods go missing in transit
scenarios.how: Loads are short-delivered or diverted.

scenarios.name: High-value materials are stolen by organised groups
scenarios.how: Copper, cable, fuel or similar are stolen with insider help.

scenarios.name: Consumables and spares are pilfered
scenarios.how: Small items disappear without records.

scenarios.name: Losses are never tracked
scenarios.how: Shrinkage and losses are written off without analysis.

scenarios.name: An email account is taken over
scenarios.how: A mailbox without strong sign-in is used to send or intercept payment instructions.
scenarios.why: Most business email compromise starts with an account that has no multi-factor authentication.

scenarios.name: A payment instruction received by email is acted on
scenarios.how: Changed details or urgent payments are processed on the strength of an email.
scenarios.why: Acting on payment instructions received by email is how business email compromise succeeds.

scenarios.name: A cloned voice or video instruction is obeyed
scenarios.how: A caller who sounds or looks like a known person is believed.
scenarios.why: Voices and faces can be cloned, so only an agreed verification method holds.

scenarios.name: Customer accounts are taken over
scenarios.how: Stolen passwords or SIM swaps are used to drain customer accounts.
scenarios.why: Customer accounts without takeover protection are drained with stolen passwords.

scenarios.name: A security compromise is not notified
scenarios.how: The Regulator and affected people are not told, so they cannot protect themselves.
scenarios.why: POPIA section 22 requires notification as soon as reasonably possible.

scenarios.name: A help desk reset hands an attacker access
scenarios.how: An impersonator persuades the help desk to reset a password or authenticator.

scenarios.name: Systems that move money are accessed without strong sign-in
scenarios.how: Remote access, cloud or banking systems rely on passwords alone.

scenarios.name: Personal information is over-exposed or kept too long
scenarios.how: Too many people can reach or export personal information, or records outlive their purpose.

scenarios.name: A SIM swap defeats one-time PIN approvals
scenarios.how: Approvals sent by SMS are intercepted.

scenarios.name: An AI assistant is manipulated by hidden instructions
scenarios.how: Instructions planted in emails or documents make an assistant leak data or act.

scenarios.name: The organisation's own information helps attackers
scenarios.how: Published staff details and routines make impersonation easier.

scenarios.name: The organisation is impersonated to defraud others
scenarios.how: Fake websites, accounts or job adverts in the organisation's name collect money or personal information.

scenarios.name: Spoofed email in the organisation's name deceives staff, suppliers or customers
scenarios.how: Emails that appear to come from the organisation's own domain carry false payment instructions.

scenarios.name: A compromise is not contained quickly
scenarios.how: Accounts stay compromised while suppliers and customers keep receiving instructions.

scenarios.name: Concerns are never reported
scenarios.how: People who suspect fraud have no safe route, or do not know whom to tell.
scenarios.why: Tips are the most common way fraud is detected, and safe routes decide whether people report.

scenarios.name: A reporter is exposed or retaliated against
scenarios.how: A reporter's identity leaks or they are penalised, and others stop reporting.
scenarios.why: Confidentiality and protection from retaliation decide whether anyone reports again; reporter confidentiality added after the review's isolated-weakness probe.

scenarios.name: A company has no confidential disclosure system
scenarios.how: A public or state-owned company does not maintain and publicise the system section 159(7) requires.
scenarios.why: A statutory duty for public and state-owned companies.

scenarios.name: Evidence is lost before it is secured
scenarios.how: The people involved are alerted before emails, devices and logs are preserved.
scenarios.why: Evidence lost in the first days of a case usually cannot be recovered.

scenarios.name: An investigation is not independent or fair
scenarios.how: The investigator is too close to the matter, or conclusions ignore other explanations.

scenarios.name: Allegations are lost or mishandled at intake
scenarios.how: Reports are not logged, anonymous ones are set aside, or urgent containment waits.

scenarios.name: Fraud is found only by accident
scenarios.how: Nobody looks for fraud proactively, or alerts are acted on without checking the facts.

scenarios.name: Disclosure timelines are missed
scenarios.how: Reporters are not told within the statutory periods what will happen.

scenarios.name: Consequences and recovery are inconsistent
scenarios.how: Discipline, criminal reporting and recovery depend on who is involved.

objectives.name: Ownership and accountability
objectives.purpose: Whether a named person owns fraud risk with the authority to act on it, and whether roles across the organisation are clear.

objectives.name: Oversight by the board or council
objectives.purpose: Whether the governing body sees fraud risk, incidents and losses often enough, and in enough detail, to hold management to account.

objectives.name: Oversight in an owner-managed organisation
objectives.purpose: Where the owners run the business themselves, the same oversight has to come from the owners and from someone outside day-to-day operations.

objectives.name: Oversight within a group
objectives.purpose: Where oversight sits with a parent company or head office, whether group requirements reach this organisation and whether someone locally is still accountable.

objectives.name: Fraud policy and response plan
objectives.purpose: Whether the organisation has stated what it expects, what counts as fraud, and what happens when fraud is suspected.

objectives.name: Legal and regulatory obligations
objectives.purpose: Whether the organisation knows and meets its legal duties to report and prevent fraud and corruption. Sector-specific duties appear only where they apply.

objectives.name: Resourcing, assurance and insurance
objectives.purpose: Whether fraud risk work is planned, staffed by capable people, independently checked, and backed by insurance that would actually pay.

objectives.name: The organisation's own use of AI
objectives.purpose: Whether the AI tools the organisation itself relies on are governed, so they cannot be used to commit fraud or be manipulated into enabling it.

objectives.name: Monitoring and improving the programme
objectives.purpose: Whether the organisation measures how well it manages fraud risk and learns from what goes wrong.

objectives.name: Gateway
objectives.purpose: Establishes whether the organisation has assessed its fraud risks and how. Organisations without a structured assessment take a short clarification route; those with one are tested on its quality.

objectives.name: Fraud risk awareness in management
objectives.purpose: A short route that records why fraud risk has not been assessed and whether management has any working view of where fraud could happen.

objectives.name: Linking known fraud risks to controls
objectives.purpose: Whether the ways fraud could happen, however they were identified, are tied to controls that would stop or detect them.

objectives.name: Ownership and participation
objectives.purpose: Whether management owns the assessment and whether the people who know how processes really work take part in it.

objectives.name: What the assessment covers
objectives.purpose: Whether the assessment covers the whole organisation, every type of perpetrator and every major type of fraud, including newer threats.

objectives.name: How fraud risks are identified
objectives.purpose: Whether risks are described as specific schemes and drawn from the organisation's own experience, outside intelligence and data, so that controls can be tested against them.

objectives.name: How fraud risks are rated
objectives.purpose: Whether each risk is rated consistently for likelihood and harm, before and after controls, and compared with the organisation's tolerance.

objectives.name: Linking risks to controls
objectives.purpose: Whether each fraud risk is matched to the controls meant to stop or detect it, and whether those controls are known to work, including against AI fakes.

objectives.name: Acting on the results
objectives.purpose: Whether the assessment leads to decisions and completed actions, and whether it directs audit, detection and training effort.

objectives.name: Keeping the assessment current
objectives.purpose: Whether the assessment is refreshed regularly and whenever the business, its systems or the threats it faces change.

objectives.name: Documentation and connections
objectives.purpose: Whether the assessment is documented well enough to defend, known to the people it concerns, and connected to the organisation's other risk work.

objectives.name: Code of conduct
objectives.purpose: Whether the organisation has written down the behaviour it expects, made it reach everyone who acts for it, and enforces it consistently.

objectives.name: Tone at the top and ethical culture
objectives.purpose: Whether leaders model the standards they set, whether integrity counts in appointments and performance, and whether the organisation knows what its culture is really like.

objectives.name: Conflicts of interest across the organisation
objectives.purpose: Whether everyone, not only buyers, declares interests and relationships that could influence their decisions, and whether declarations are checked and acted on. Procurement-specific declarations are covered in D4.

objectives.name: Gifts, hospitality and entertainment
objectives.purpose: Whether gifts and hospitality, given and received, are limited, recorded, approved and reviewed so they cannot be used to influence decisions.

objectives.name: Anti-bribery procedures
objectives.purpose: Whether the organisation has the procedures that would support an adequate procedures defence: a clear prohibition, a view of where bribery risk sits, guidance for staff who face a demand, and checks on payments that could hide a bribe. Due diligence on agents and intermediaries is covered in D4.

objectives.name: Extortion and disruption at projects and sites
objectives.purpose: Whether the organisation has a safe, lawful and recorded way to respond when groups demand payments or a share of the work under threat of disruption.

objectives.name: Donations, sponsorships and social investment
objectives.purpose: Whether money given away for good causes is approved, checked for links to decision-makers and confirmed as used for its purpose, so it cannot serve as a disguised bribe.

objectives.name: Dealing with government and officials
objectives.purpose: Whether contact with officials is transparent, whether bids are honest and independent, and whether submissions to the state are accurate.

objectives.name: Integrity rules for public sector organisations
objectives.purpose: Whether the integrity obligations that apply specifically to the public sector are met and checked.

objectives.name: Operating across borders
objectives.purpose: Whether the anti-bribery programme reaches every country the organisation works in and reflects foreign laws that may apply to it.

objectives.name: Targets, incentives and pressure
objectives.purpose: Whether the way performance is rewarded creates pressure to cut corners, and whether results that trigger rewards are checked.

objectives.name: Training and awareness
objectives.purpose: Whether everyone, and especially people in high-risk roles, knows the standards, recognises the frauds they are likely to face, including AI-enabled ones, and knows what to do.

objectives.name: Monitoring the ethics programme
objectives.purpose: Whether the organisation checks that its ethics and anti-bribery measures work and improves them after allegations.

objectives.name: How buying is organised
objectives.purpose: Factual questions that switch the later modules on or off, so the organisation only sees what applies to it.

objectives.name: Policy, authority and separation of duties
objectives.purpose: Whether rules exist for who may commit the organisation's money, and whether one person can control a purchase from start to finish.

objectives.name: Supplier onboarding and vetting
objectives.purpose: Whether a supplier must prove it is real, properly owned and correctly banked before it can be paid, and whether that holds over time.

objectives.name: Supplier bank detail changes
objectives.purpose: The most common route for redirecting supplier payments. Questions follow the primary control in depth, and fall back to compensating controls when it is missing.

objectives.name: Competitive sourcing and bids
objectives.purpose: Whether competition is genuine: thresholds hold, bids are protected, evaluation is independent and exceptions are controlled.

objectives.name: Purchase orders and approval
objectives.purpose: Whether the organisation is committed only after approval, and whether limits can be worked around.

objectives.name: Receiving goods and services
objectives.purpose: Whether the organisation confirms it actually received what it pays for.

objectives.name: Invoices and payment release
objectives.purpose: The last point at which a false or inflated claim can be stopped before money leaves.

objectives.name: Agreed prices and changes
objectives.purpose: Whether what is paid matches what was agreed, and changes are approved first, whether or not there is a written contract.

objectives.name: Contract management
objectives.purpose: Whether the organisation pays what it agreed to, and whether contracts grow only with approval.

objectives.name: Conflicts of interest and supplier relationships
objectives.purpose: Whether personal interests and gifts that could bias buying decisions are declared, checked and acted on.

objectives.name: Purchase cards and petty cash
objectives.purpose: Whether low-value buying channels outside the normal process are limited and reviewed.

objectives.name: Monitoring and assurance
objectives.purpose: Whether anyone would notice if the controls above failed.

objectives.name: Agents, intermediaries and outsourced providers
objectives.purpose: Third parties beyond ordinary suppliers: people who act in the organisation's name, and providers that run a process handling its money, customers or data. Asked whatever the procurement route.

objectives.name: Paying individuals without a payroll
objectives.purpose: A short route for organisations with no employees, which still pay contractors or casual helpers.

objectives.name: Recruitment and screening
objectives.purpose: Whether only real, approved positions are filled, and whether the people appointed are who they say they are.

objectives.name: Employee records and pay changes
objectives.purpose: Whether someone could add a fictitious employee, redirect a salary or raise pay without a second person noticing.

objectives.name: Payroll run and payment
objectives.purpose: The checks between calculating the payroll and money leaving the bank, where a manipulated run or payment file would be caught.

objectives.name: Oversight of an outsourced payroll
objectives.purpose: When someone else runs the payroll, the controls that matter are the instructions you send, the report you check and who releases the money.

objectives.name: Leavers and terminations
objectives.purpose: Whether pay stops when employment stops.

objectives.name: Time, attendance and leave
objectives.purpose: Whether people are paid only for time actually worked and leave actually approved. Hours-based questions appear only where pay depends on hours or shifts.

objectives.name: Temporary and labour-broker workers
objectives.purpose: Whether the organisation pays only for workers who were actually there, at the agreed rate.

objectives.name: Expenses, allowances and advances
objectives.purpose: Whether claims and advances are supported, approved by someone independent and recovered.

objectives.name: Cash wages
objectives.purpose: Cash wages are among the easiest payments to divert, so they need physical controls at payout.

objectives.name: High-risk roles and privileged access
objectives.purpose: Whether the organisation knows which roles could commit or conceal fraud, gives those roles stronger controls, and watches the people who can change systems, data and payments.

objectives.name: Mandatory leave and rotation
objectives.purpose: Whether people in sensitive roles step away often enough, and work changes hands often enough, for hidden schemes and long-standing collusion to come to light.

objectives.name: Behavioural and lifestyle indicators
objectives.purpose: Whether warning signs in behaviour are recognised and raised fairly, whether pressure on employees is reduced before it turns into fraud, and whether lifestyle reviews follow a lawful process.

objectives.name: Payroll verification and monitoring
objectives.purpose: Whether anyone would notice a ghost employee, a redirected salary or a quiet pay increase if the controls above failed.

objectives.name: Bank accounts, mandates and company records
objectives.purpose: Whether the organisation knows every account it holds, controls who can act on them at the bank, and would notice if someone took over its accounts or its company record.

objectives.name: Banking platform and payment release
objectives.purpose: Whether the banking platform enforces separation and dual approval for every payment, including beneficiaries and once-off payments, and whether those controls hold when an instruction seems to come from the top.

objectives.name: Branch and cash payments
objectives.purpose: Where payments are made by branch instruction or cash, whether two people control them and every withdrawal is accounted for.

objectives.name: Reconciliations and cash management
objectives.purpose: Whether every account is reconciled by someone independent, and whether a payment made outside the normal process would show up.

objectives.name: Journals, estimates and write-offs
objectives.purpose: Whether entries made outside normal transaction processing are approved and reviewed, since this is where results are manipulated and theft is hidden.

objectives.name: Financial reporting and management override
objectives.purpose: Whether the organisation guards against results being manipulated, particularly where bonuses, covenants, funding or a sale depend on them.

objectives.name: Treasury, investments and foreign exchange
objectives.purpose: Whether deals are authorised within limits, confirmed and settled by people independent of the dealer, and whether balances are confirmed with the institutions.

objectives.name: Tax, VAT and the SARS profile
objectives.purpose: Whether refunds can be diverted through a hijacked eFiling profile, and whether VAT claims and returns are reviewed.

objectives.name: Grant and donor funds
objectives.purpose: Whether restricted money is spent as the funder intended, each cost is claimed once, and reports to funders match the books.

objectives.name: Oversight of small, outsourced or group finance
objectives.purpose: Where one or two people, an outside firm or a group runs the money, whether the owners or management keep enough sight of it to notice a problem.

objectives.name: Finance automation and AI tools
objectives.purpose: Whether automated and AI tools used in finance are checked by people and protected from changes that would let errors or fraud through.

objectives.name: Monitoring, assurance and payment recall
objectives.purpose: Whether unusual payments would be spotted, whether controls have been independently checked, and whether the organisation can act fast when a fraudulent payment goes out.

objectives.name: Income from other sources
objectives.purpose: A short route for organisations without paying customers, which may still receive income that could be diverted.

objectives.name: Customer onboarding and identity
objectives.purpose: Whether the organisation knows who its customers really are before it supplies goods, services or credit, including when customers sign up remotely.

objectives.name: FICA customer due diligence
objectives.purpose: For accountable institutions, whether customer due diligence works as a fraud control as well as a compliance requirement.

objectives.name: Credit, applications and collections
objectives.purpose: Whether credit is granted only to genuine, verified applicants by someone independent of sales, and whether customer payments reach the right account and invoice.

objectives.name: Pricing, discounts and special terms
objectives.purpose: Whether prices and discounts can be changed only within approved limits, and whether unrecorded promises to customers are prevented.

objectives.name: Refunds, credit notes and returns
objectives.purpose: Whether money or credit given back to customers is genuine, approved independently and paid to the right place.

objectives.name: Billing, receipting and sales integrity
objectives.purpose: Whether everything supplied is billed, every payment is receipted and banked, sales are genuine, and customers are protected from criminals pretending to be the organisation.

objectives.name: Agents, resellers and sales channels
objectives.purpose: Whether sales reported through commissioned channels are real before commission is paid. Vetting of agents is covered in D4.

objectives.name: Promotions, loyalty, vouchers and gift cards
objectives.purpose: Whether value given away through promotions reaches genuine customers, and whether staff cannot award it to themselves.

objectives.name: Customer claims
objectives.purpose: Whether claims are checked against the terms, screened for fraud indicators and supporting evidence, and paid only to verified parties.

objectives.name: Monitoring and customer fraud response
objectives.purpose: Whether losses from customer fraud are visible, customers can report fraud, and revenue controls have been independently checked.

objectives.name: Physical exposure
objectives.purpose: Establishes which physical things of value the organisation holds or moves: cash, stock, assets, vehicles and fuel, scrap, goods in transit and high-value materials.

objectives.name: Cash handling and banking
objectives.purpose: Whether cash is controlled by two people at every hand-over, reconciled daily, banked intact and checked by someone who does not handle it.

objectives.name: Stock control and storage
objectives.purpose: Whether stock can leave only against an approved record, whether the people who hold it are separate from those who record it, and whether high-value items get extra protection.

objectives.name: Stock counts, losses and write-offs
objectives.purpose: Whether counts are independent and frequent enough to expose losses, and whether write-offs cannot be used to cover theft.

objectives.name: Consumables and spares
objectives.purpose: A short route for organisations that hold only small quantities of consumables or spares.

objectives.name: Dispatch and goods in transit
objectives.purpose: Whether what leaves the organisation matches what was ordered, arrives where it should, and cannot be diverted on the way.

objectives.name: Fixed and portable assets
objectives.purpose: Whether the organisation knows what it owns, where it is and who has it, and whether missing assets are investigated.

objectives.name: Disposals, scrap and by-products
objectives.purpose: Whether assets and scrap leave at a fair value, to the right buyer, with every kilogram and rand accounted for.

objectives.name: Vehicles, fleet and fuel
objectives.purpose: Whether fuel is bought only for the organisation's vehicles and work, vehicles are used as intended, and maintenance costs are genuine.

objectives.name: Organised theft of high-value materials
objectives.purpose: Whether the organisation treats organised theft of metals, cable, fuel and similar materials as a fraud and security risk, often involving insiders.

objectives.name: Monitoring and assurance
objectives.purpose: Whether losses of physical value are visible over time and controls have been independently examined.

objectives.name: Email and payment-instruction fraud
objectives.purpose: Whether staff email accounts are hard to take over, the organisation's name is hard to spoof, and an instruction received by email is never enough on its own to move money or change details.

objectives.name: Impersonation, deepfakes and verification
objectives.purpose: Whether the organisation has a verification habit that holds when a voice, face or message seems genuine, and whether it can respond when criminals pretend to be the organisation.

objectives.name: System access and authentication
objectives.purpose: Whether the accounts that can move money or change data are hard to take over, and whether administrator, help desk and provider access cannot be abused.

objectives.name: SIM swaps and one-time PINs
objectives.purpose: Whether a criminal who takes over a cellphone number can use it to approve payments or reset access.

objectives.name: Digital customer channels
objectives.purpose: Whether customers' accounts and transactions on the organisation's digital channels are protected from takeover, automated attack and manipulation of AI assistants. Remote onboarding is covered in D7.

objectives.name: Personal information and data leakage
objectives.purpose: Whether personal information that criminals could use for impersonation or sell on is protected from insiders and outsiders, and whether a compromise is reported as POPIA requires.

objectives.name: What the organisation reveals about itself
objectives.purpose: Whether the organisation and its people give criminals the information they need to choose whom to impersonate and whom to target.

objectives.name: AI assistants and agents
objectives.purpose: Controls for AI tools that read the organisation's information or act on its behalf.

objectives.name: Reporting and response
objectives.purpose: Whether a suspected cyber-enabled fraud is reported and contained within minutes, and whether defences have been independently tested.

objectives.name: Detection and response set-up
objectives.purpose: Establishes the organisation's size, who investigates suspected fraud, what speak-up channel exists, whether company or public sector disclosure duties apply, and whether there has been a recent case.

objectives.name: Speak-up channels
objectives.purpose: Whether the channel is easy and safe to use for everyone who might know about fraud, in their own language, at any hour, and keeps anonymous reporters in the conversation.

objectives.name: Where there is no formal channel
objectives.purpose: A short route that records whether people know what to do and whether a channel is planned.

objectives.name: Protecting people who speak up
objectives.purpose: Whether reporters' identities are protected, retaliation is prevented and punished, and the organisation meets its legal duties to respond.

objectives.name: Case intake and management
objectives.purpose: Whether every allegation, from any source, is logged, assessed, assigned to someone independent and driven to a conclusion.

objectives.name: Proactive detection and analytics
objectives.purpose: Whether the organisation looks for fraud itself, aims its tests at its main risks, closes every exception, and keeps its detection current as AI changes how fraud is committed.

objectives.name: Investigations
objectives.purpose: Whether investigations are done by capable, independent people following a procedure that will stand up in a disciplinary hearing, a civil claim or a criminal court.

objectives.name: Evidence and digital forensics
objectives.purpose: Whether evidence is preserved before suspects are alerted, handled so that it is admissible, and examined by specialists when it may have been fabricated. Asked of every organisation, because evidence has to be preserved whoever investigates.

objectives.name: Consequences, reporting and recovery
objectives.purpose: Whether confirmed fraud leads to consistent discipline, criminal reporting and determined recovery, and whether outcomes are recorded.

objectives.name: The most recent case
objectives.purpose: Factual questions about the most recent case. They show how fraud is actually found and handled here, and are compared with industry patterns in the report.

crossObjectives.name: Changes to payment details are verified through a route the requester does not control
Money leaves only with two independent approvals, enforced where it leaves
Identity is established through routes an impersonator cannot control
Payment files cannot be altered between approval and the bank
Accounts are confirmed as belonging to the payee
Documents are verified with their source, not on appearance
Automated and AI decisions are reviewed by a person and their permissions limited
Signals and alerts prompt fair review, never a verdict
Interests are declared and conflicted people kept out of decisions
Records are kept for justified periods, held when needed and access restricted
Weaknesses behind a loss are fixed

D4-V-06.why: Bank-enforced two-person authorisation of every payment includes supplier payments.

D5-P-05.why: Bank-enforced two-person authorisation of every payment includes salary payments.

D5-O-09.why: Bank-enforced two-person authorisation of every payment includes salary payments released by the organisation.

boundaries.D1: Covers accountability, oversight, policy, legal reporting duties and the organisation's own AI. Does not assess corporate governance generally or legal compliance beyond fraud-related duties.
boundaries.D2: Covers whether fraud risks are recognised, linked to controls and acted on. Does not rate the quality of enterprise risk management generally.
boundaries.D3: Covers bribery, conflicts, gifts, extortion, public-sector integrity and conduct expectations. Does not assess employment relations or broader ESG performance.
boundaries.D4: Covers buying, supplier onboarding and bank details, payment, contracts and outsourced providers. Does not assess value for money or supplier performance beyond fraud indicators.
boundaries.D5: Covers hiring, payroll, leavers, time, expenses, brokers and insider risk, with fair-treatment safeguards. Does not assess HR practice or labour-law compliance generally.
boundaries.D6: Covers bank accounts, payment release, reconciliations, journals, reporting manipulation, SARS profile and restricted funds. Does not audit financial statements or tax compliance.
boundaries.D7: Covers onboarding, credit, refunds, billing, claims, agents and customer fraud response. Does not assess credit risk, pricing strategy or consumer-protection compliance generally.
boundaries.D8: Covers cash, stock, assets, disposals, dispatch, fleet and organised theft. Does not assess physical security design or health and safety.
boundaries.D9: Covers email compromise, impersonation, access, SIM swap, customer channels, personal information exposure and AI assistants. Does not test technical security or assess IT general controls generally.
boundaries.D10: Covers speak-up, reporter protection, intake, detection, investigation, evidence and consequences. Does not decide guilt, protected status, liability, an adequate-procedures defence or entitlement to pension deductions.
